Situation1: Got a request to attend court to provide testimony when required.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They raise concerns about a policy that seems to disadvantage certain youth, seniors, or refugee applicants.
Story: I sat in my office, the crisp police uniform feeling heavier than usual. The court summons lay on my desk, a reminder of my duty to provide honest testimony about a recent arrest. As a police officer, I was expected to act with integrity and fairness, to present the facts without bias. But as an advocate, I had spent months challenging the very policy that led to this arrest—a policy that, in my view, unfairly targeted refugee youth. My colleagues in advocacy expected me to speak out, to use my voice to highlight the flaws in the system and push for change. Yet, the department and the court demanded strict adherence to the facts, no editorializing, no personal opinions. The weight of both uniforms pressed on me, each demanding loyalty, each with its own code. My mind raced with the possible consequences—betraying my fellow officers, letting down the youth who looked to me for hope. I stared at the clock, knowing the moment of truth was coming, and I still didn’t know which part of myself would take the stand.
